However, during the development of GUI agents for dynamic scenarios, error compounding leads to a labor-intensive and expensive bottleneck, requiring high costs for manual intervention. Meanwhile, errors are hard to be located and difficult to track failure reasoning. Consequently, it is challenging to overcome random errors simply by blindly increasing the size of the training dataset and address errors in a targeted manner. Existing research primarily attempt to improve GUI agent by optimizing the agent&apos;s internal design to avoid outcome deviation, ignoring the critical need for automated self-correction in step-level agent errors. In view of this, we propose the Automated Oversight (AO), an efficient four-stage closed-loop approach designed to emulate human-level oversight. The architecture consists of four key phases: (1) global outcome verification for final-state checking; (2) step-level visual trajectory alignment to intercept errors in real-time; (3) teacher-driven root-cause diagnosis to analyze failures; and (4) closed-loop rectification with state rollback to recover the task. Unlike traditional methods, AO focuses on failure-aware reasoning to identify the root causes of errors and execute targeted recovery. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method can improve agent success rates and reduce human cognitive burden by achieving reliable autonomous interactions in dynamic systems. However, during the development of GUI agents for dynamic scenarios, error compounding leads to a labor-intensive and expensive bottleneck, requiring high costs for manual intervention. Meanwhile, errors are hard to be located and difficult to track failure reasoning. Consequently, it is challenging to overcome random errors simply by blindly increasing the size of the training dataset and address errors in a targeted manner. Existing research primarily attempt to improve GUI agent by optimizing the agent&apos;s internal design to avoid outcome deviation, ignoring the critical need for automated self-correction in step-level agent errors. In view of this, we propose the Automated Oversight (AO), an efficient four-stage closed-loop approach designed to emulate human-level oversight. The architecture consists of four key phases: (1) global outcome verification for final-state checking; (2) step-level visual trajectory alignment to intercept errors in real-time; (3) teacher-driven root-cause diagnosis to analyze failures; and (4) closed-loop rectification with state rollback to recover the task. Unlike traditional methods, AO focuses on failure-aware reasoning to identify the root causes of errors and execute targeted recovery. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method can improve agent success rates and reduce human cognitive burden by achieving reliable autonomous interactions in dynamic systems. We will publicly release our code.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6991012\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/978-94-011-3488-0_8\", \"title\": [\"What Are the Limitations of the Situation Calculus?\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-011-3488-0_8\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[1991]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1017/cbo9780511576430.008\", \"title\": [\"Limitations\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511576430.008\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2009, 3, 12]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202512.1743.v1\", \"title\": [\"Reflective Reasoning System: Inference-Time Self-Diagnosis and Self-Correction for Large Reasoning Models\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) often exhibit an efficiency-accuracy trade-off, leading to errors from insufficient self-diagnosis and correction during inference. Existing reasoning methods frequently lack internal feedback for refining generated steps. To address this, we propose the Reflective Reasoning System (RRS), an inference-time framework integrating explicit self-diagnosis and self-correction loops into LRM reasoning. RRS strategically employs meta-cognitive tokens to guide the model through initial reasoning, critical self-assessment of potential flaws, and subsequent revision, all without requiring additional training or fine-tuning. Our extensive experiments across diverse open-source models and challenging benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and scientific reasoning demonstrate that RRS consistently achieves significant accuracy improvements compared to baseline models and competitive inference-time enhancement methods. Human evaluations and ablation studies further confirm the efficacy of these distinct self-diagnosis and self-correction phases, highlighting RRS's ability to unlock LRMs' latent reflective capabilities for more robust and accurate solutions.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202512.1743.v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 12, 19]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "ffed88430b1729b911a0b2121d130052f14c3ddbced76b19b655f7371a79d9a0", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "assumption_challenge", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6991012", "doi:10.1007/978-94-011-3488-0_8", "doi:10.1017/cbo9780511576430.008", "doi:10.20944/preprints202512.1743.v1"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6991012", "https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-011-3488-0_8", "https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511576430.008", "https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202512.1743.v1"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
